# singleflight, MQ and Event Streams

## Category

database / cache subtree. Node position: three mechanisms that "let requests take a detour around the direct path" — singleflight merging source fetches, MQ peak shaving, event stream fan-out — and their shared ledger: trading semantics for throughput.

## Definition


This page discusses three mechanisms that "let requests take a detour around the direct path": singleflight merges concurrent duplicate source fetches into a single one; a message queue turns "finish it right now" into "queue it up and work through it slowly"; and an event stream fans one business action out into multiple downstream consumers. What they have in common is that they all buy the system time or exchange for decoupling, and what they share as risk is that semantics get blurred — who consumed what, in what order, how many times, is often impossible to state clearly.

## Problem

Merging source fetches, queueing for deferral, and fanning out consumption all buy the system time or exchange for decoupling, and the shared risk is that semantics get blurred: who consumed what, in what order, how many times, is often impossible to state clearly. A hot-key breakdown amplifies a single expiry into a single incident; a queue turns "done" from milliseconds into queue depth divided by consumer speed, and the backlog is still invisible; at-least-once delivery means duplication is inevitable — idempotency is not optional, it is consumer-side infrastructure.


### Why a hot-key breakdown is an amplifier problem

A cache expiry itself is not scary; what is scary is the expiry happening on a hotspot. The instant a key that is read tens of thousands of times per second expires, every request discovers at once that there is no cache, and at once hammers the source. The source normally only needs to absorb one percent of the traffic, and at that moment it has to absorb all of it; overload slows the source fetch, and the slower source fetch piles up even more requests. The essence of a breakdown is not "queries got slow" — it is a single expiry being amplified by concurrency into a single incident.

Common defense ideas:

- Allow only one request to fetch from the source, and have the rest wait for it to fill the cache back.
- Make hot keys logically never expire, refreshed asynchronously by the background.
- Warm up before release or server opening, leaving no window for a breakdown.
- Also cache a short-lived empty value for data that does not exist, avoiding repeated punches through to the source.

These ideas do not conflict with each other; they are usually stacked according to the degree of hotness.

### The idea of singleflight: merge source fetches rather than reject requests

singleflight's core action is plain: concurrent source fetches for the same key let only one go out, and everyone else shares its result. It drops no request and reports no error; it simply folds "ten thousand identical queries" into "one query plus ten thousand result distributions".

This idea holds on its own apart from any specific library, and applies wherever duplicate work exists:

- The same player's profile is fetched from the source simultaneously in hundreds of requests.
- The same configuration is pulled simultaneously by dozens of processes.
- The same aggregate result is recomputed simultaneously by multiple timers.

Its boundary is equally worth remembering: merging only helps for exactly identical queries — if the parameters differ even slightly, each fetches its own source; and the side waiting to share a result ties its latency to the first request, so if the first request fails the waiters fail together, which means waiters usually need their own timeout and fallback read. Spreading this idea onto high-duplication paths outside the cache often yields more benefit than guarding a single hot key.

### The essence of peak shaving: trading instantaneous latency for long-term stability

The most cited value of a message queue is peak shaving. When a traffic surge arrives, requests no longer press directly onto the handler; they land in the queue first, and the handler consumes at its own pace. The peak is flattened, but the cost is equally real: the time until an operation is complete goes from milliseconds to "queue depth divided by consumer speed".

So whether peak shaving pays off depends on the business's tolerance for how long "done" takes:

- Telemetry, logs and achievement statistics — a few seconds, or even a few minutes, late is usually imperceptible, so queuing suits them.
- Reward issuance, orders, currency changes — the player is staring at the screen waiting for a result, so it is often not suitable to put the confirmation path into a queue.
- For operations in between, the common practice is to finish the critical step synchronously and queue the rest for asynchronous completion.

A queue has another hidden cost: the backlog is invisible. Normally consumption outpaces production and everyone assumes the queue is instantaneous; one day production overtakes it, the backlog quietly climbs to millions of messages, and by the time it is found the window for a calm response has usually already passed.

### The semantics of decoupling: the publisher no longer knows and does not care who consumes

The value of decoupling is that publishers and consumers can evolve independently: the publisher only declares "what happened" and does not care who cares; adding or removing consumers does not drag the publisher's release rhythm along. This shrinks the surface area of cross-team interfaces dramatically, and it is the genuine organizational gain of event-driven architecture.

But decoupling also splits responsibility. The publisher can no longer guarantee "the downstream is done", and several questions surface with it:

- If consumption fails, who is responsible? How many retries, and after failure go to a dead letter or discard outright.
- Will a message be delivered more than once? Almost certainly, at least during retries and consumer-group rebalances.
- Can the consumer keep up? When it cannot, whose alert does the backlog go to.

The usual convention at a mature team: the publisher guarantees the message is reliably sent out, the consumer guarantees idempotent consumption, and monitoring in between turns backlog, failure and latency all into explicit metrics. Whichever link lacks a convention is the link that becomes an incident at some point in the middle of the night.

### Why ordering is hard to guarantee in an event stream

An event stream unfolds one action into several consumers each handling it separately, and ordering problems come with it. There is concurrency on the publishing side, partitions in the queue, retries on the consumer side — any one of these links can turn "deduct then ship" into "ship then deduct".

Common ordering traps:

- Using the player as a partition key guarantees per-player ordering, but ordering across players is no longer guaranteed.
- When a failed consumption is retried, later messages have already been processed, and the retried one becomes a late, stale event.
- The same entity's state is maintained separately by two consumers, each seeing a different order.

The common practice is not to chase global ordering — global ordering usually means a throughput ceiling — but to narrow the ordering requirement down to "within the same entity", satisfied by a partition key or an in-entity version number. The remaining cases that truly need cross-entity ordering usually mean those two actions should be merged into one piece of processing, rather than hoping the queue lines them up for them.

### Idempotency is the consumer side's responsibility

Message systems generally promise "at least once delivery", which translates as "duplication may happen". So idempotency is not optional icing on the cake, it is consumer-side infrastructure: processing the same message twice must give the same result as processing it once.

Common handles for implementing idempotency:

- Use a business order number or event ID as a deduplication key, and check "was this done" before processing.
- State updates carry a precondition, and states already advanced are skipped outright.
- Money and asset operations carry a unique constraint when written to the database, leaving the database as the final backstop.

Problems usually arise not in the main flow but in the compensation flow: manually supplementing messages, replaying historical partitions, and consumer scaling triggering a rebalance can all feed messages from several days ago back into the consumption logic. Idempotency must be designed on the assumption "this message may come back at any time", not on "under normal conditions it only comes once".

### Common pitfalls

- Treating peak shaving as free benefit and also stuffing player-perceptible critical paths into the queue to wait.
- Assuming the queue neither duplicates nor reorders, leaving deduplication and ordering to luck.
- Using singleflight only for cache source fetches, while configuration pulls and timed aggregations — equally high-duplication paths — each do their own thing.
- Retrying failed consumption without limit, so one poison message stalls the consumption progress of the whole partition.

Every mechanism in this group trades semantics for throughput, and what is worth thinking through before trading is: which semantics the business truly depends on, and which are only assumptions that implementation happened to carry along.

## Used By
